Crop
crop
n. (the craw or first stomach of a bird); v.t. (to cut off the top; to pluck)
Saxon crop, the top or head of a plant, and also the craw of a fowl. Both senses survive in the Authorized Version: the bird's craw in Leviticus, and the verb to crop off a tender twig in Ezekiel.

Biblical Definition

The noun belongs to the poor man's offering. When a worshipper could not afford a lamb he brought turtledoves or young pigeons, and the priest “shall pluck away his crop with his feathers, and cast it beside the altar on the east part, by the place of the ashes” (Lev 1:16) — the crop being the bird's craw, the pouch that holds what it has eaten off the ground. Even in the cheapest sacrifice in the law, the refuse is removed before the offering ascends. God does not become less particular as the offering becomes less costly; the poor man's dove is prepared with the same care as the bullock. The verb appears in Ezekiel's parable of the cedar, and it is Messianic: “I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent” (Eze 17:22). God Himself does the cropping. A tender shoot is taken from the top of a felled royal house and planted on a high mountain, and it becomes a great tree sheltering every fowl — the Davidic line cut down to a stump and raised again in Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines crop as the first stomach of a fowl, the craw; the top or highest part of a plant; and as a verb, to cut off the ends, to pluck, to mow or reap.

expand to see more

CROP, n. [Sax. crop, the top or head of a plant, also the craw of a fowl.]

1. The first stomach of a fowl; the craw.

He shall pluck away his crop with his feathers. Lev. 1.

2. The top or highest part of a plant; the end or shoot.

3. That which is gathered; the corn or fruits of the earth collected. CROP, v.t. To cut off the ends of any thing; to pluck; to mow or reap.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 1:16 — "And he shall pluck away his crop with his feathers, and cast it beside the altar on the east part, by the place of the ashes:"

Ezekiel 17:22 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD; I will also take of the highest branch of the high cedar, and will set it; I will crop off from the top of his young twigs a tender one, and will plant it upon an high mountain and eminent:"

Leviticus 1:14 — "And if the burnt sacrifice for his offering to the LORD be of fowls, then he shall bring his offering of turtledoves, or of young pigeons."

Isaiah 53:2 — "For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, he shall not desire him."

Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is as exact about the poor man's offering as about the rich man's.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody is contesting the word. What Leviticus 1:16 holds is a principle the church loses in both directions. The bird offering existed because some worshippers could not afford a lamb; the law made a way for the poor man to come. And yet the law does not become casual because the offering is cheap — the crop and the feathers are removed, the ashes have a place, the east side is specified. Mercy toward the poor and exactness in worship are not in competition. A congregation that thinks care about the ordinances is a luxury of the comfortable has misread the cheapest sacrifice in the book.

The principle to recover, then, is the regulative instinct applied evenly: God says how He will be approached, and He says it as carefully to the man with two pigeons as to the man with a bullock. Ezekiel 17:22 carries the same word into prophecy, and there the tenderness is the point — a tender one cropped from the top of a ruined house and planted by God on a high mountain. Isaiah saw the same shoot: he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground. The cropping looks like loss, and it is how the kingdom came.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew mur'ah (H4760), the crop or craw of a bird; qataph (H6998), to pluck off; Saxon crop, the top of a plant or the craw of a fowl.

expand to see more

Hebrew mur'ah (H4760) — the crop, craw of a bird; Leviticus 1:16, and found nowhere else in Scripture.

Hebrew notsah (H5133) — the feathers or plumage cast aside with it.

Hebrew eqtoph (H6998) — I will crop off, pluck; Ezekiel 17:22, with God as the one plucking.

Hebrew rak (H7390) — tender, soft; the young shoot of Ezekiel 17:22 and the tender plant of Isaiah 53:2.

Saxon crop — the top of a plant, the craw of a fowl; Webster's root, holding both senses at once.

Usage

"“Pluck away his crop with his feathers” — the poor man's offering, prepared with full care."

"“I will crop off… a tender one” — and God is the one doing the cropping."

"“As a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground” — the same shoot, seen by Isaiah."
